title: Session routing to AWS Lambda MicroVMs with Amazon CloudFront, Lambda@Edge and Amazon DynamoDB
description: Route each request to its own per-session AWS Lambda MicroVM. A session id in the path or query selects the VM; Lambda@Edge routes and a control-plane Lambda launches it.

introBox.headline: How it works
text: This pattern gives every session its own AWS Lambda MicroVM behind a single Amazon CloudFront URL. A request carries its session id in the path (/s/{sessionId}/...) or, as a fallback, the query string (?session={sessionId}). An Amazon DynamoDB table maps each session id to the MicroVM currently serving it (endpoint, auth token, state).

A Lambda@Edge origin-request function runs on the default behavior. It reads the session record from DynamoDB: if the MicroVM is usable it rewrites the origin to the VM endpoint (and the Host header, which does not auto-follow), attaches the proxy auth token, and forwards the stripped path on port 8080. If not, it 307-redirects to a regional control-plane Lambda that launches the MicroVM (or attaches to the running one), then bounces the viewer back to retry.

The control plane uses a conditional DynamoDB write as a launch lock, so concurrent first requests for a session start one MicroVM, not several. The app inside each MicroVM is a Node.js hello-world that returns its own session id, so /s/A and /s/B land on two different MicroVMs. There is no authentication (the session id is the only key), so this is a demo, not a production design.

bullets.text: Restrict access to an AWS Lambda function URL origin (CloudFront Origin Access Control)

text: Open https://<distribution>.cloudfront.net/s/session-a/ and /s/session-b/ (for example with curl -sL) and confirm each response comes from a different MicroVM. See the README for the full steps.
CloudFront takes a few hours to delete the Lambda@Edge replicas, so the first destroy usually ends in DELETE_FAILED on the edge function. Wait a few hours and run npx cdk destroy again.
